Two big steps remain, according to Le: the current version relies on a laser, and it would need to become a fully electronic device. The color range would also need to widen, which may require changing the device's structure. Whether it can become a commercial product is still an open question.
technology.originalTitle: New rewritable displays can show an image for months without power

technology.headline: IBM and University of Chicago Quantum Computer Completes Hard Task With Verified Results
summary: Researchers at IBM and the University of Chicago report that an IBM quantum computer finished an extremely complex calculation in about 15 minutes. They say the leading ways of simulating that calculation on conventional computers would take impractically long. The team also found a way to build statistical confidence that the quantum computer's answers were accurate, which has been one of the field's biggest obstacles.

The team describes the result as meeting the basic criteria for quantum advantage: doing a task beyond the practical reach of classical methods while producing results that can be trusted. To get there, they designed a more structured version of a common benchmark called random circuit sampling. This structure lets errors be detected during the computation. The experiment used 70 protected logical qubits, 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical T gates. Encoding the circuits gave logical error rates 10 times lower than the underlying physical error rates. The researchers have made their circuits and results publicly available through the Quantum Advantage Tracker.
technology.bigPicture: The experiment was meant to demonstrate quantum advantage, not to solve an everyday real-world problem. Even so, it tackles two things needed for large-scale quantum computing: keeping errors under control and knowing whether the answers can be trusted. If these methods continue to work as machines grow, quantum computers could one day help with scientific and industrial problems that are currently out of reach. That remains a possibility, and the researchers describe this result as a step in that direction.
technology.originalTitle: IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes

technology.headline: Lab-built 'active' materials can crawl, walk and dig using their own internal energy
summary: Most everyday materials, like metal, glass, concrete and rubber, only change shape when something outside pushes or pulls on them. Researchers from the universities of Amsterdam, New South Wales and Cambridge have been building a different kind of material, called active matter, which carries its own source of energy. They made it from simple parts such as small motors, rods and rubber bands, and their work has led to two recently accepted scientific papers.

In the first study, the team linked rods into a flexible chain and placed small motors at the joints. The motors made the links uneven, so moving one rod affected its neighbor differently than the reverse. Where an ordinary material would bend and snap just once, these chains could buckle and snap again and again. That repeated motion can look like crawling, walking or even digging. The work appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
technology.bigPicture: These findings suggest that how parts are connected can matter as much as how strong or active each part is. The researchers say the chain results point toward materials that could do several jobs on their own, and that could be useful in soft robots whose bodies produce complex movements without a central control system. They also believe the second finding could help in understanding and designing systems made of tiny active structures, such as biological gels, sheets of closely connected cells and networks that mimic aspects of biological information processing. These are possibilities, and the work so far is based on laboratory structures built from simple parts.
technology.originalTitle: Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures

technology.headline: Laser 'printing' of steel could help repair aging bridges instead of replacing them
summary: The U.K. has about 300 million metric tons of iron and steel in its buildings and transport infrastructure, and many structures are older than people realize. A report from the Royal Academy of Engineering warned that action is urgent. Repairs and replacements need more steel, and making or recycling steel carries a climate cost, even with lower-carbon methods.

One option is additive manufacturing, which builds objects layer by layer. In a method called wire-fed laser-directed energy deposition, a thin metal wire is fed into a laser beam. The beam melts the wire and a small patch of the old steel, so new metal bonds directly to the original and is added only where it is needed. Siemens and Fastech already offer additive manufacturing for onsite repairs of other equipment, such as steam turbine rotors.
technology.bigPicture: If repairs like this prove reliable, they could help keep older bridges and buildings in use longer. The article says that keeping just 1% of the U.K.'s steel stock in service could avoid 3 million metric tons of new steel production. It also says focused renovation can produce 84%–93% lower emissions than replacement and can let bridges stay open. Before that can happen, engineers need to learn how old and new steel behave together, so they can judge how much extra safe life a repair really adds.
technology.originalTitle: Technology for 'printing' steel could help extend the life of aging bridges and buildings

technology.headline: Rice University Team Makes Fast-Charging Battery Graphite in Just 0.2 Seconds
summary: Many lithium-ion batteries, including those in cars, phones and cameras, use graphite in one of their electrodes, called the anode. When a battery charges, lithium ions move into this graphite, and how fast they can travel through it is a key limit on charging speed. A research group led by James Tour at Rice University has now made a synthetic graphite that supports much faster charging.

The method starts with petroleum coke, a low-cost carbon leftover from oil refining, mixed with a small amount of a nickel compound. One short, powerful electrical pulse heats the mixture to about 2,500°C, and the carbon quickly arranges itself into orderly graphite layers. The whole process takes two-tenths of a second, whereas making graphite normally takes long periods of very high heat.
technology.bigPicture: Charging speed and the cost of making battery materials are both big concerns for electric vehicles, and this work tackles them together. If the approach holds up beyond the lab, it could possibly lead to batteries that charge faster and are cheaper and cleaner to produce. The researchers also found that the nickel's main job is helping build the graphite structure, since the benefits stayed even after more than 99% of the leftover nickel was removed. That finding may guide future work on making materials with less energy, though the material's real-world performance still needs to be shown.
technology.originalTitle: New synthetic graphite paves way for rapid EV charging

technology.headline: Prototype drone folds its arms to squeeze through gaps about half its width
summary: A team of researchers in Europe has built a prototype drone whose side arms fold when they touch the edges of a narrow opening. The drone shrinks from 12.3 inches (31.3 cm) wide to 5.6 inches (14.1 cm), a 55% reduction. Earlier folding drones had managed up to 29%. Unlike many past designs, it has no dedicated motors for folding, which keeps it simpler.

The team found the design using an automated search. Computer simulations tested candidate shapes and joint stiffness, including how the arms touch edges, fold, pass through an opening and recover. The best candidate at each step guided the next round. The finished drone uses 3D-printed parts and spring-loaded joints that stay rigid in normal flight but bend on contact. In flight tests it crossed a 5.9-inch (15 cm) gap at roughly 4.5 mph (2 m/s) and passed through a 15.7-inch-long tube. It also handled angled approaches to a 7.9-inch gap without problems up to 20°, though an arm slipped out of place once at 30° and several times at 35°.
technology.bigPicture: Drones are often sent into places that are hard for people to reach, and those places can include tight or oddly shaped openings. A simple passive design that folds on contact, without extra motors, could be one way to help drones fit through such spaces. The researchers suggest that more accurate simulations might lead to designs that perform even better in the real world. This is still an early prototype, though, and the rough crossings and arm slips at steeper angles show there is more work to do.
technology.originalTitle: New drone prototype folds itself through gaps half its width during flight

ai.headline: Survey: Three in four Australians have mistaken AI-made content for real
summary: A representative survey of 2,000 Australian adults, carried out in August and September 2026, found that 76% had recently come across content they first thought was real and later learned was made by AI. Most Australians have used or tried generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini. About half (51%) use them at least weekly, 28% use them daily, and 96% know of at least one platform.

The people most likely to say they had been fooled were those with high education and high AI literacy. The researchers suggest this is because these people are better at noticing when they have been misled. People with low education and lower AI literacy were the most likely to say they did not know whether they had been fooled.
ai.bigPicture: The findings suggest many people may not realise when they have met AI-made content, even as more of them turn to AI tools for information. When people suspect something is AI-generated, most just look closer and trust their own judgment. Few check labels or independent sources, and this approach may work less well as AI content becomes more convincing. The authors argue for clearer and more consistent labeling by digital platforms, and for media and AI literacy education for adults as well as children. If those steps were taken, people might find it easier to judge what they see online.
ai.originalTitle: 76% of Australians are struggling to tell apart real and AI content

ai.headline: Auckland Team's AI Dance Partner Shows a Different Way to Build AI
summary: Researchers in an Auckland dance studio spent 10 months building an AI dance partner in extended reality, which blends the physical world with digital elements. The partner was an architectural avatar, a digital structure that moved in response to a dancer. A choreographer, an architectural designer and two professional dancers developed and tested it. The dancers wore motion-capture suits tracked by 10 cameras, and the AI learned from their movements instead of from text.

The team found that a small set of choreographed duets taught the system better than a large library of generic movement. Mixing dance styles produced bland, in-between moves, and for most of the project the partner could only follow. They also noticed that when the system stopped responding to a dancer's small gestures, the dancer stopped making them. The dancers kept ownership of their data, recordings stayed on local encrypted drives, and any choreography was credited as a joint creation.
ai.bigPicture: The authors contrast their approach with companies racing toward "superintelligence," which rely on more data, computing power and scale. They suggest that keeping skilled people closely involved could make AI more accountable, and that a smaller country could build AI suited to its own users. They also say New Zealand's light-touch regulation could change, perhaps giving skilled people a say in how AI is used in areas like health, justice, education and welfare. The study is one small example, and the authors say the open challenge is whether institutions will recognize and reward alternatives like it.
ai.originalTitle: We built an AI you can dance with. It taught us about developing the technology responsibly

ai.headline: Tooth-mounted sensor lets people give silent commands to AI by mouthing words
summary: Researchers at ETH Zurich have developed InvisiSpeech, a small device that sits between a back molar and the cheek and picks up silent speech. The wearer shapes words with their tongue as usual, without making a sound or moving their lips. This creates tiny vibrations in the mouth, which the sensor detects and sends wirelessly to a smartphone. An AI model built by the researchers then decodes the words and carries out the command.

In a study with 15 people, the system correctly recognized about 90% of 50 preset English commands after a short calibration for each person. Background noise had little effect, which the researchers say is an advantage over microphone-based systems. Tested uses included switching devices on and off, looking up information during a meeting, and translating foreign-language content with AI glasses. The device does not read brain signals, and it can be put in and taken out without surgery.
ai.bigPicture: The team hopes silent speech could one day allow natural, private conversations with AI, with answers delivered through earphones, for example on a train or while commuting. They also suggest it could help with everyday tasks, accessible communication and controlling AI glasses. For now, the device is still in development. The researchers say it needs to handle longer, more complex sentences and work reliably when the wearer is walking or moving quickly before it is practical for everyday use.
ai.originalTitle: A gadget straight out of a James Bond film: Tiny tooth-mounted sensor recognizes silent speech

ai.headline: Los Angeles Schools Turn Off Google's AI Search Summaries as Dispute With Google Grows
summary: Los Angeles Unified, the district with half a million students, has quietly turned off Google's AI Overview summaries in searches on school-issued devices. It did not make a formal announcement, and parents and students were caught off guard. The change came on the Monday after a Friday, Nov. 13 meeting of the school board's AI committee, where members of the group Schools Beyond Screens LA spoke. The district said the suspension is temporary and meant to keep student experiences age-appropriate and safe.

The step comes amid a wider standoff. Google has said it cannot separate AI from its search product. A Google education executive told The New York Times that if schools ban AI, students will not have access to search. In early November, Google said it would turn off Gemini and search tools by default for K-12 schools in the coming months, so administrators would need to switch each one on. Some Google employees signed a petition asking the company to let schools turn off AI without losing search, and other districts, such as Fairfax County in Virginia, have built plug-ins that remove AI summaries. Google has offered a pilot "guided learning" tool rather than an AI-free search for schools.
ai.bigPicture: Google's Chromebooks and education apps are widely used in American classrooms, so this disagreement affects many schools. Districts may keep looking at other search providers or at their own technical workarounds, and Google could come under more pressure to offer a version of search without AI. How the dispute is settled might shape how much control schools have over the AI tools their students see. For now, it is unclear how long Los Angeles will keep the feature disabled or how it was done.
ai.originalTitle: As Google threatens to cut schools' search access, Los Angeles blocks AI features

ai.headline: Anthropic CEO rejects claim he wants people to give up free will to AI
summary: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, said on Wednesday that he does not think humans should hand over their free will to AI systems. In a long post on X, he called the suggestion "absurd" and wrote that legitimacy and self-determination should never be given up for the sake of efficiency or security. The post came a week after Anthropic's record-setting stock market debut.

He was responding to an Axios article on the AI debate. Without naming anyone, he criticized "some AI CEOs" who say AI should be just a tool but do not do anything different in their products. Meta's chief AI officer Alexandr Wang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have both recently said similar things about keeping human agency. Elon Musk reposted Amodei's statement with the single word "interesting."
ai.bigPicture: This exchange shows that leading AI companies are publicly working out how much control machines should have and how much should stay with people. Anthropic's IPO filing says each new Claude version speeds up development of the next, and that Claude wrote over 90% of the contributions to its codebase in September. That makes the question of limits on self-improving AI more concrete. If the companies spell out where those limits sit, it could shape how future products are built and how the public judges them. For now, the lines remain unspecified, so it is unclear what any limits would look like.
ai.originalTitle: Anthropic chief denies wanting humans to 'surrender' free will to AI

ai.headline: Singapore's Punggol Digital District Serves as a Real-World Testing Ground for Robots and AI
summary: In a government-built district called Punggol Digital District, Singapore is trying out technology that could become part of daily life. In a staged demonstration, AI-powered cameras and sensors spotted a coffee spill at an office block. A cleaning robot then left its dock, rode an elevator to the eighth floor and cleaned up the mess without human help.

The district covers 50 hectares and has eight businesses and office blocks, a mall, a university campus and a metro station. A central digital platform gathers data from thousands of cameras and sensors, and AI analyzes it, with human operators helping. The system can respond to problems, anticipate disruption and cut energy use and waste. For example, it can reduce elevator movements when demand is low and adjust air-conditioning in real time. Staff also use a digital replica of the district on a giant screen to spot or predict problems.
ai.bigPicture: Testing robots and connected systems across a whole district, rather than in separate places, may help companies see how the technology works in everyday settings. A Panasonic executive said similar trials in Japan took longer because he had to deal with many separate building managers, regulators and agencies. If the approach works, it could possibly help cities cope with fewer workers while keeping public spaces clean and safe. Safety rules are still being developed, and the people interviewed said they had no privacy worries, so how these tools are received more widely remains to be seen.
ai.originalTitle: Robots roam Singapore's urban AI testing ground

ai.headline: AI-made holiday ads promote products that don't exist, leaving shoppers with losses
summary: Short vertical video ads made with artificial intelligence are drawing millions of views ahead of Black Friday. They promote items such as themed Advent calendars, heated robes and pet accessories. Experts say holiday gift scams are not new, but AI has made it cheaper to produce a convincing product demonstration. In an October 2026 shopping survey, 43% of Americans said they had been fooled by ads created with the technology.

Shoppers describe a range of problems. Content creator Maggie McGaugh, who makes unboxing videos about these items, says what arrives is usually much smaller and poorer in quality than the ads suggest. One shopper, Tia Evans, paid more than $200 for four robes after seeing the ad repeatedly. The website then went dark and her messages went unanswered. Another, Michelle Richard, is still waiting for her order. H&M said its name was falsely used to promote products it does not sell. Some shoppers also reported that their card details were misused on gambling websites.
ai.bigPicture: The story shows how cheap AI tools can make a fake product look real, and how seeing an ad many times can make it feel trustworthy. Digital media expert Christina Inge describes the holiday season as a "perfect storm" for impulse buying. Shoppers may need to be more careful about unfamiliar sellers and to check payment protections before buying. Retailers whose names are misused could also face pressure to respond, though the article does not say what may happen next.
ai.originalTitle: Fake gifts, real losses as AI ads proliferate

ai.headline: Study finds AI can often identify 'anonymous' speakers from small personal details
summary: Researchers at Northeastern University, Tianshi Li and Jianing Wen, tested how well AI can work out who someone is from an interview with the obvious clues removed. They picked 822 people with known identities from Reddit's "Ask Me Anything" community and turned their backgrounds into fictional interviews about work and technology. Names and other clear giveaways were taken out. The strongest AI systems still identified the speaker in roughly 400 of the interviews, often by combining details that seem harmless alone, such as a job description, a project and the years spent on it.

Web access helped the AI, but it was not essential: three models still named 15% to 28% of speakers using only what they learned in training. When the bots reported high or very high confidence, about nine in ten answers were right. In a second test on 143 interviews with even more clues removed, the AI still identified 85.3% of speakers. Telling the AI to protect identities did not fix the problem, because its web searches surfaced pages that named the speaker, and those links could be seen in the results. The researchers then trained another AI model to flag revealing passages, and removing them cut the average success rate from 75.1% to 35.1% on the smaller test set.
ai.bigPicture: Experts quoted in the article say anonymous data has never been as simple as removing a few identifiers, but AI makes re-identification cheaper and easier for people without special skills. That could mean people who once spoke freely on message boards face a higher risk of being exposed. The same methods might also help people decide what to share or keep separate across accounts, help developers build tools that warn about risky details before something is posted, and help police trace anonymous threats or protect victims and witnesses. Research like this could also give the public stronger grounds to ask lawmakers for privacy protections.
ai.originalTitle: Think you're anonymous online? AI can blow your cover

ai.headline: Study Says Common AI Buzzwords May Mislead the Public About What the Technology Does
summary: Researchers at Simon Fraser University say the words the AI industry uses may be confusing people about how the technology works and what harm it can cause. In a study published in the journal AI and Ethics, they call this practice "glosslighting." The term combines a glossary of words with gaslighting, meaning manipulating how people understand something. The authors argue that vague, abstract language helps shape public opinion, hide harms and avoid scrutiny.

The team gives a couple of examples. Saying data lives in "the cloud" skips over the large, energy-intensive data centers and server farms that store and process it. Calling a chatbot's false output a "hallucination" makes it sound humanlike and suggests a simple slip, rather than a systemic error a company should answer for. The study was led by assistant professor Nicholas Vincent, with computing science student Ayana Hussain and Ph.D. candidate Weina Jin. Vincent says most of their suggested alternative terms would make communication easier, though some may need extra explanation.
ai.bigPicture: The researchers say more precise wording could make AI companies more transparent and accountable. It could also challenge the idea that ever more powerful AI is inevitable. Vincent suggests that as shoppers become pickier, they may ask for clearer descriptions of what an AI product actually is. If that happens, it could encourage plainer language, but the study does not say whether the industry will change how it talks.
ai.originalTitle: 'Glosslighting' the public: Study calls for overhaul of industry-led AI buzzwords

ai.headline: Study of Sierra Leone teachers suggests chatbots could be a cheaper route to information than web search
summary: Researchers studied how teachers in Sierra Leone used an AI chatbot called theTeacher.AI, which works inside WhatsApp like any other contact. More than 500 teachers were trained to use it, and over 100 of them answered a survey. The idea behind the study is that although mobile phones are common in Africa, only 37% of people there use the internet. Many of those who do go online prefer social networking apps to search engines, partly because search results lead to large foreign websites that use up costly data.

Among the teachers surveyed, 77% said they used the chatbot for information about teaching, 69% used books and 37% used the internet. Almost 70% of the questions they asked were for facts or concepts, a common use of search engines elsewhere. The authors calculated that an average web page needs 718 times more data to load than an AI response, which makes the chatbot 98% cheaper, even when computing costs are included. Use of the tool did fall over time, though. Across all trained teachers, the share using it dropped from 62% in the first month to 19% in the 17th month, which suggests the first version may not have been useful over the long term for most of them.
ai.bigPicture: Where data is scarce and expensive, a chatbot that needs far less bandwidth than a web page could be a practical way to get information. The findings hint that some regions might rely on AI tools instead of traditional web search, as some places skipped older technologies before. The steep drop in use over 17 months shows that low cost alone may not keep people engaged. Whether tools like this become lasting resources could depend on how well they meet users' needs over time.
ai.originalTitle: Chatbots may leapfrog web search in sub-Saharan Africa

ai.headline: MIT Study Suggests Brains May Process Many Languages in a Similar Way
summary: Researchers at MIT studied people who speak 21 different languages and found signs that the brain may handle language in a shared, universal way. Languages vary a lot. Vietnamese uses pitch to change meaning, for example, and Russian allows more flexible word order than English. Even so, the team reports something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates. The work was published in Nature Neuroscience, and Evelina Fedorenko of MIT's McGovern Institute for Brain Research is the senior author.

The team used multilingual AI models, which turn words and phrases into numbers that represent their meaning. They combined those numbers with brain scans to build tools that predict how a brain will respond to a given piece of language. The lab already had scan data from speakers of 12 languages and recruited speakers of nine more. Those volunteers listened to stories from "Alice in Wonderland" in their native language while their brain activity was recorded. The resulting prediction tools worked accurately in all of the languages studied. The researchers say this is the first study to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages.
ai.bigPicture: Most earlier tools of this kind existed for only a handful of languages, such as English, French and Chinese. This study suggests they can be extended to many more, including understudied ones. The researchers note that AI language tools are being developed to help diagnose brain disorders, and this work could let speakers of more languages benefit from them. They also say it may one day help keep endangered languages from vanishing. These outcomes are possibilities rather than results, and they would need further research.
ai.originalTitle: Many languages, one common neural code

ai.headline: AI tool spots possible bladder cancer warning signs in health records years early
summary: Researchers at the University of Plymouth have built an AI system that searches electronic health records for patterns that could point to bladder cancer before a diagnosis is made. In some patients, it picked up subtle signals dating back as far as five years. The team studied records from nearly 70,000 patients covering 1995 through 2020. The model, called PRECISE-AGZ, looked at 48,261 possible health indicators and narrowed them to 38 that were most useful for predicting risk.

The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and correctly classified 91% of those who did not. It also did better than existing NHS referral guidelines, and it worked effectively as early as 12 months before diagnosis. It confirmed known risk factors such as smoking and blood in the urine, and it also found unexpected links. Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared linked to lower risk, while long-term use of the breast cancer drug tamoxifen was linked to higher risk. The researchers stress this does not mean one condition protects against bladder cancer or that tamoxifen causes it. The tool can also sort patients into low-risk, uncertain and high-risk groups.
ai.bigPicture: Bladder cancer has no routine screening program for the general population, and confirming it currently means an invasive camera examination called cystoscopy. A tool like this could, if further research confirms it works, help doctors decide who needs urgent testing and who might be monitored first. That might mean earlier detection and fewer unnecessary procedures. For now the technology is not ready for widespread clinical use, because all the data came from one database in Wales and the model must be tested on other patient groups and record systems.
ai.originalTitle: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

ourworld.headline: Endangered Leatherback Turtles Are Nesting in New Places Along Ecuador's Coast
summary: Researchers recorded an unprecedented number of eastern Pacific leatherback nests on several Ecuadorian beaches during the 2025-2026 nesting season. These beaches are more than 1,000 miles from the turtles' traditional nesting areas in Mexico and Costa Rica. Leatherbacks are the world's largest sea turtle, and this population is critically endangered. It has dropped by more than 90% since the 1980s.

The team reviewed more than 45 years of records from Ecuador's coast and compared them with El Niño and La Niña cycles. Over the past decade, turtle activity and nesting rose during La Niña, when the water is cooler. Eggs per nest and hatching success were similar to those at the established northern sites, and some nests produced more hatchlings than usual. One female, nicknamed Bella, was tracked nesting four to five times in 2026. Streetlights confused her on her first attempt, but two nights later she nested on a quieter stretch of beach. In all, 134 of her 146 eggs hatched, a rate of 91.8%.
ourworld.bigPicture: The researchers suggest the turtles may be responding to warming oceans by looking for cooler coastal waters, though this is an interpretation of the pattern rather than a proven cause. The study's lead author describes the findings as a sign of hope, but the population still faces serious threats. These include accidental capture in fishing gear, plastic pollution, boat collisions, egg harvesting and damage to nesting habitat. He says long-term survival would likely depend on continued monitoring, steps to reduce accidental catches, and careful care of coastal areas, with local communities involved. If protections for these new beaches are put in place, they could become a valuable refuge, but that is not guaranteed.
ourworld.originalTitle: Facing extinction, the world’s largest sea turtle is making a surprising move

ourworld.headline: Hera's first images show a stadium-sized crater on asteroid Dimorphos
summary: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached the asteroid pair visited by NASA's DART probe, which hit the small asteroid Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022. That impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit by 33 minutes, much more than predicted. Until now, scientists did not know whether the impact had left a crater, changed the asteroid's shape, or changed nothing at all. Hera's first images suggest the answer is all three together.

The face DART struck has been flattened into a crater about the size of a sports stadium, stretching across the asteroid's whole width. The rest of Dimorphos looks much as it did in DART's 2022 images. Hera also shows that Dimorphos is now tumbling wildly in its orbit. In addition, hundreds of previously unknown boulders, each just a few meters across, circle the two asteroids. The team will need to account for them as Hera moves closer.
ourworld.bigPicture: The DART mission showed that an asteroid's orbit can be changed, and Hera is now showing what the impact did to the asteroid itself. Mission leaders say this could help make asteroid deflection a more reliable tool for protecting Earth, though that is a goal and not yet a proven capability. Hera is due to move to about 13 km from the pair in December. Two small CubeSats are planned for January 2027, one of which will use radar to probe an asteroid's interior for the first time. A separate ESA mission, Ramses, is being developed to study the asteroid Apophis during its safe close pass of Earth in 2029.
ourworld.originalTitle: Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact

ourworld.headline: Antarctic ozone hole is among the largest in decades, but recovery stays on track
summary: This year's ozone hole over Antarctica is one of the biggest seen in the 48 years of observations. That is a sharp change from 2025, when it was the fifth smallest since 1992. By Sept. 20, 2026, it covered 27.3 million square km (10.5 million square miles), which is larger than Antarctica itself. That is about 31% above the 20-year average for that time of year.

Researchers point to an unusually strong and long-lasting polar vortex. It kept the Antarctic stratosphere cold enough for ozone loss to continue for longer. Data from the Copernicus Sentinel-5P satellite also show that the hole was not especially deep. Ozone depletion stayed close to average, so the hole was wide but not as deep as other large ones on record.
ourworld.bigPicture: The size of the ozone hole changes naturally from year to year, so one large season does not by itself mean the ozone layer has stopped recovering. Long-term recovery is described as on track following the global phaseout of ozone-depleting substances under the Montreal Protocol. Satellites like Sentinel-5P build steady records that help scientists tell normal ups and downs from longer-term trends. Newer missions, including Sentinel-5 and Altius, could help track the ozone layer's recovery more accurately in the coming years.
ourworld.originalTitle: Ozone hole one of the largest in decades

ourworld.headline: Astronomers find the most distant quasar yet, from the universe's early days
summary: A German-led team has reported the most distant quasar known so far. A quasar is the bright core of a galaxy with a black hole at its center. This one is seen as it was about 630 million years after the Big Bang, roughly 13.1 billion years ago, when the universe was less than 5% of its present age.

The team, led by Julien Wolf of the European Southern Observatory, found it while searching through a huge number of observations from the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope. Hubble, Webb and other observatories confirmed the result. Webb data showed that the black hole has a mass equal to about 360 million Suns, even though it takes in surrounding material fairly slowly.
ourworld.bigPicture: Finding such a large black hole so early in the universe raises a puzzle that Wolf put simply as "but how?" Studying this object could help researchers test ideas about how black holes grew so large so soon after the Big Bang. The record may not last long, though. Wolf said it could be broken within months or could stand for years, so more distant discoveries remain possible.
ourworld.originalTitle: Scientists discover quasar formed within a mere 630 million years of the Big Bang, setting a record

ourworld.headline: Strange trenches on Australia's Nullarbor Plain point to hidden collapsing caves below
summary: Researchers have worked out what created long, shallow trenches scattered across the Nullarbor Plain in southern Australia. The plain covers more than 200,000 square kilometers and is one of the world's largest areas of limestone. The trenches run roughly north-south, reach up to 20 km in length and are only a few meters deep. They are almost invisible from the ground but show up clearly in digital landscape models.

The trenches look a little like flat-bottomed valleys, but rivers did not make them. They start and stop abruptly, are not linked to drainage networks and contain no sign of sediment left by flowing water. To find the cause, the team combined drone and aerial photos, satellite-based landscape models, measurements from boreholes and caves, and geophysical methods that let them see inside the ground.
ourworld.bigPicture: Knowing where hidden voids lie underground can matter for planning buildings, roads, tunnels and sewers, for reducing geological hazards, and for protecting groundwater. Caves can also preserve records of ancient environments and shelter unusual life forms, so finding them is a first step toward studying them. The authors suggest the same approach might help spot caves on other planets such as Mars, where caves could be possible places to look for life or to base future explorers. They say similar trenches have probably been overlooked in other places, though how many hidden cave systems exist is not yet known.
ourworld.originalTitle: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds

ourworld.headline: Mystery object called Phoebe could be a black hole from the early universe
summary: On December 18, 2019, astronomers saw a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way, slowly brighten for about an hour and then return to normal. The change was smooth and symmetrical, with no explosion or flare. It looked as if an unseen object had passed in front of the star and bent its light toward Earth, an effect called gravitational microlensing. Researchers at Swinburne University in Melbourne spotted the signal in survey data and named the object Phoebe.

The team found three possible explanations. Phoebe could be a rogue planet drifting alone through the Milky Way, or a similar wandering planet inside the Large Magellanic Cloud. In the second case, it would be the first planet found by microlensing beyond our galaxy. The third option is a primordial black hole, which would have formed in the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang, long before the first stars.
ourworld.bigPicture: If Phoebe turns out to be a primordial black hole, it could be one of the oldest objects ever detected, and it might offer new clues about dark matter. For now, its identity is still uncertain, and the rogue planet explanations remain possible. Further observations and analysis could help show which explanation fits best. The result also shows how a single brief change in a star's brightness can open a window onto very large questions about the universe.
ourworld.originalTitle: Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

ourworld.headline: California Prepares for Flooding as Very High Tides Meet El Niño Storms
summary: Californians are getting ready for a combination of unusually high tides and El Niño-driven weather during Thanksgiving week, the busiest travel week of the year in the U.S. Forecasters said seawater could spill into low-lying parts of the San Francisco Bay Area on Wednesday and Thursday. The National Weather Service's Dial Hoang said flooding could reach nearly 3 feet (0.9 meters) at the Wednesday peak, and that this year's tides are expected to be the highest since January 1983.

The weather service also warned of dangerous breaking waves of up to 30 feet (9 meters) on Wednesday, with hazardous beach conditions lasting through Sunday. San Francisco International Airport officials said its runways are no longer at risk of flooding, but authorities still encouraged residents to rethink holiday travel. Mayor Daniel Lurie called the situation "extremely serious" and urged people not to drive through floodwaters. He also noted that strong winds could bring down trees and that waterfront streets can flood even with little rain.
ourworld.bigPicture: King tides happen every year because of the positions of the Earth, moon and sun, and more are expected in December and January. This year the ocean is also warmer than usual, which makes it expand, and that can add to flood risk when tides are high. A coastal oceanographer said the last time tides this high met El Niño storms, the damage ran to hundreds of millions of dollars. The state may fare better this time thanks to storm preparation and infrastructure improvements, though risks remain, and the coming months could show how well those measures hold up.
ourworld.originalTitle: California braces for flooding threat from huge tides, El Niño

ourworld.headline: China Sends First Foreign Astronaut, from Pakistan, to Its Space Station on Shenzhou 24
summary: China launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft on Wednesday morning from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the northwest of the country. On board were Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, along with Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40. The craft separated from its rocket, reached its planned orbit, and the crew later entered the space station, where they posed for group photos with three astronauts from the Shenzhou 23 mission. It was the first joint flight of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's crewed space program.

The crew is set to carry out more than 90 science experiments and technology tests. Ali will run an experiment on photosynthetic cyanobacteria during his short stay, then return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft. This is the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, while Tang has flown twice before and is now the first astronaut to board the Tiangong station three times. Tang said differences in language, culture and psychology made teamwork harder, but that efforts on both sides were paying off. Ali spoke in Mandarin at a news conference and quoted a line of Chinese poetry.
ourworld.bigPicture: The flight is part of an agreement China and Pakistan signed in February 2025, and leaders in both countries described it as a milestone for their relationship. Ali said he hopes cooperation could grow from one astronaut on one flight to several joint flights, and perhaps to the moon and Mars. A Pakistani minister said the day Pakistan sends astronauts on its own will come, though no timeline was given. The mission also comes as China prepares for a crewed lunar landing by 2030, while NASA aims to land astronauts on the moon in 2028.
ourworld.originalTitle: China launches Shenzhou 24 spacecraft carrying 2 Chinese and 1 Pakistani astronaut

ourworld.headline: Euclid Space Telescope Finds Its First New Comet While Studying Distant Galaxies
summary: The European Space Agency's Euclid telescope has spotted a comet nobody had seen before, the first found by the mission. Euclid was built to photograph far-off galaxies, not to follow fast-moving objects in our own solar system. The comet showed up in images taken between September 16 and 24, 2026. It is now listed officially as C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

Mikko Pöntinen, a PhD student at the University of Helsinki, found it using software he wrote to track small solar system objects. The program flagged a streak across several images, and he then located the object in five image sets, 16 exposures in total. A fuzzy cloud around it suggested a comet shedding dust and gas. After checking catalogs of known asteroids and comets, he reported it to the Minor Planet Center, which confirmed the discovery on October 8 after further observations from telescopes on Earth.
ourworld.bigPicture: Comets are leftovers from the early solar system, so studying them may help scientists learn about the conditions when planets formed, and possibly about the origins of Earth's water and the chemical building blocks of life. This comet is not a suitable target for ESA's future Comet Interceptor mission. Even so, the quick detection and alert gave the two mission teams a real test of how they might work together. In the future, that kind of cooperation could possibly help pick targets for later missions.
ourworld.originalTitle: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected

ourworld.headline: Strong El Niño Quiets Atlantic Hurricane Season While Pacific Sets Activity Record
summary: The 2026 hurricane season ends on Nov. 30, and it showed a sharp split between two ocean basins. The Atlantic had 10 named storms, below the usual 14, and only one of them, Isaias, became a hurricane. Isaias was also the Atlantic's only major hurricane, with top winds of 120 mph. It came ashore on Oct. 9 near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 storm and brought storm surge, damaging winds and flooding rain to parts of the Southeast.

The Pacific was far busier. The eastern Pacific had 20 named storms, 10 of them hurricanes, including eight major ones. Hurricane Polo was the season's most intense storm, and its central pressure of 892 mb was the second lowest ever observed in that basin. Combined with the central Pacific, the region recorded its most active season on record, with an accumulated cyclone energy of 359.5, compared with the old record of 318 in 2018.
ourworld.bigPicture: This season shows how one climate pattern can push storm activity in opposite directions in different parts of the world. A quiet Atlantic year still brought serious damage from a single hurricane, which supports the warning that it only takes one storm to make a bad season. Forecasters say they plan to study the results of their new models more closely, and that work could possibly lead to further improvements in future warnings. Communities in Hawaii and elsewhere may also draw lessons from this year as they prepare for coming seasons.
ourworld.originalTitle: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Niño fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic

ourworld.headline: Atom-sized black holes could destroy stars from inside, new simulations suggest
summary: Researchers at MIT and other institutions have studied whether primordial black holes, which may have formed just after the Big Bang, could destroy stars. In their model, a black hole about the size of an atom but with the mass of an asteroid becomes trapped inside a star like our Sun. It then sinks to the core and starts feeding on the material around it. The work was published in The Astrophysical Journal.

A star on its own generally could not capture such a black hole, the team found. A companion star or planet could change the gravity enough to trap it, and the black hole could then pass through the star many times, losing energy through friction. Over several million years it could consume about 1 percent of the star's mass. If the star spins fast enough, the falling gas would form a disk around the black hole. Lead author Ore Gottlieb says this would doom the star, as powerful jets could make it explode within a few dozen seconds.
ourworld.bigPicture: Primordial black holes have not been confirmed, and they are one proposed explanation for dark matter. The researchers predict the explosion would show up first as X-rays and gamma rays, then as optical, infrared and radio light. Such a signal might be visible to telescopes already in use, even from galaxies far away. If astronomers did spot this pattern, it could offer a new way to look for these black holes and might shed light on dark matter, though that remains a possibility rather than a result.
ourworld.originalTitle: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

ourworld.headline: Webb telescope image shows hot dust in the Cassiopeia A supernova remnant
summary: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has captured a high-resolution, mid-infrared image of Cassiopeia A, also known as Cas A. The image, released on Nov. 23, 2026, shows the hot dust that makes up this supernova remnant. A remnant like this is made of the gas and dust left behind after a massive star explodes.

Scientists say the makeup of the dust offers clues about the structure of the star that created Cas A. The Webb data supports one scenario in which the inside of the star changed dramatically, possibly just hours before it exploded.
ourworld.bigPicture: Clouds of gas and dust like these will eventually help form a new generation of stars and planets, so studying them connects the end of one star's life to the beginning of others. Learning how a star's interior was arranged could help researchers better understand how massive stars change in their final moments. Further observations might add detail to this picture, though the current finding describes one possible scenario rather than a settled answer.
ourworld.originalTitle: Webb Reveals New Details in Supernova Remnant

ourworld.headline: Earth briefly had four radiation belts after the powerful May 2024 solar storm
summary: Earth is normally ringed by two doughnut-shaped zones of trapped energetic particles, called the Van Allen radiation belts, with a sparse gap between them. Researchers led by Viviane Pierrard at the Royal Belgian Institute for Space Aeronomy report the first direct observation of four separate electron belts. They appeared after the strong 'Mother's Day' geomagnetic storm of May 2024, which was the strongest storm seen in 20 years. The four belts developed in June 2024 and lasted more than four weeks, and the usual two-belt layout was back by August.

The team used a particle telescope on the PROBA-V satellite, which orbits about 820 km above Earth. To avoid being fooled by short-lived changes, they counted a belt or gap only if it lasted more than five days. Electrons from the storm moved into the usual gap, while new sparse gaps opened elsewhere and split the region into extra belts. The effect did not show up at the highest electron energies. Three-belt patterns also returned after several later storms between 2024 and 2026.
ourworld.bigPicture: Scientists have long been unsure how solar storms rearrange these belts, and earlier hints of a third belt in 2012 were not repeated in 2014–15. The researchers think electromagnetic waves probably knocked electrons out of the belts and into the atmosphere, but the exact cause is still unclear. Next, they plan to use simulations and modeling, and further observations might help separate the effects of natural waves from human radio signals, such as submarine transmitters. If that work succeeds, it could improve understanding of Earth's changing radiation environment and might support better satellite designs, radiation assessments for astronauts, and preparation for future solar storms.
ourworld.originalTitle: Four radiation belts surrounded Earth for weeks after 2024 solar superstorm

ourworld.headline: Study projects far more ground-striking lightning by 2100 if emissions stay high
summary: A new study in Earth's Future suggests that cloud-to-ground lightning could become much more common in a high-emissions future. These are the bolts that reach the surface, start wildfires and damage infrastructure such as wind turbines and power lines. Compared with 1995 to 2014, the study projects 76% to 140% more of them by the end of this century, depending on the climate model used. The researchers trained a machine learning model on 2019 lightning and climate observations, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, air pressure, wind speed and incoming sunlight.

Applied to past conditions, the model suggested these strikes rose 11% over the 20th century, or about 12% per degree Celsius of warming. Under the high-emissions scenario, that sensitivity could rise to about 30% per degree. Those figures are higher than earlier estimates, and lead author Andreas Krause said he was surprised by them. The tropics are projected to see the largest total increases, while the biggest relative jumps may come at higher latitudes, where lightning is now rare. Alaska, for example, could see 116% to 594% more.
ourworld.bigPicture: Lightning is hard to predict because it depends on both warm rising air and cold ice crystals high in the clouds, and scientists are not sure which effect will matter more. Some other studies even predict less tropical lightning, and the Amazon projections are the most uncertain. If the higher estimates were to prove correct, wildfire risk and damage to infrastructure could be affected, though the effect on human safety may depend on when during storms the extra lightning occurs. Krause also hopes to study how forests, which have adapted to their local lightning levels, might respond.
ourworld.originalTitle: Lightning could strike more than twice as often in a warming world

ourworld.headline: California Faces Flood Risk From King Tides, El Niño and Warm Oceans
summary: Forecasters say very high tides, El Niño-driven weather and unusually warm ocean water are raising the risk of coastal flooding in California during the busy Thanksgiving travel week. The San Francisco Bay Area is expected to be hit hardest. Seawater could flood low-lying areas, including the city's airport. The National Weather Service's Dial Hoang said the Bay Area could see up to nearly 3 feet (0.9 meters) of flooding when the tides peak on Wednesday.

The tides are "king tides," which happen every year because of the positions of the Earth, moon and sun. This year they are expected to be the highest since January 1983. In San Francisco they may approach or pass the record of 8.66 feet (2.6 meters), which is more than 40 years old. The National Weather Service also warned of breaking waves up to 30 feet (9 meters) on Wednesday, with hazardous beach conditions lasting through Sunday. In Southern California, surf could reach 22 feet (6.7 meters), and sneaker waves could wash beachgoers out to sea. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie called the situation "extremely serious" and asked people to limit unnecessary travel. He also warned that strong winds could bring down trees and that low-lying waterfront streets can flood with little or no rain.
ourworld.bigPicture: The article says it is not clear this week will bring the damage seen in the early 1980s, when coastal oceanographer Reinhard Flick said high tides and storms caused hundreds of millions of dollars in damage. It notes that storm preparedness and infrastructure have improved since then. The ocean is warmer and larger in volume because of human-caused climate change and this year's strong El Niño, which could make high tides reach farther. More king tides are expected around Christmas and on Jan. 21–22, and El Niño is forecast to keep strengthening through the end of the year. Flick said conditions could be quite bad if heavy rain and high waves arrive together during one of those events, but that remains a possibility rather than a certainty.
ourworld.originalTitle: California braces for triple flooding threat of huge tides, El Niño, warm oceans

ourworld.headline: Moon's far side rocks suggest asteroid impacts faded slowly rather than in one violent burst
summary: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the far side of the Moon say the evidence does not fit a long-held idea. For decades, many researchers believed the Moon was hit mainly during one catastrophic period of asteroid bombardment. The new work instead suggests that collisions became less frequent gradually, over billions of years.

The team examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for signs of ancient impacts. They identified impact events from about 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, a record covering more than three billion years. The rocks came from China's Chang'e-6 mission, the first to bring back samples from the far side. Until now, almost everything known about the Moon came from the side facing Earth.
ourworld.bigPicture: Earth has lost most of its earliest geological record to erosion, volcanic activity and moving tectonic plates, but the Moon has kept evidence of ancient impacts. Because Earth and the Moon formed together, the Moon's impact history may help scientists understand the conditions the young Earth went through. According to Dr. Jourdan, this could also shed light on the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life. Comparing far-side and near-side samples could give a fuller picture of how the early Solar System changed over time.
ourworld.originalTitle: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

ourworld.headline: Pakistani Astronaut to Join Chinese Crew Heading to Tiangong Space Station
summary: China announced the crew for its Shenzhou 24 mission on Tuesday, ahead of a launch planned for Wednesday morning from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center. Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, will fly with Chinese colleagues Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39. Ali, a former air force pilot, is set to be the first foreign astronaut to board China's space station. The flight would also be the first joint flight with Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program, under an agreement China and Pakistan signed in February 2025.

Ali will be a payload specialist on a short stay, mainly looking after experiments for the two countries' cooperation. He is due to carry out four science projects in biotechnology and materials, including one on photosynthetic microorganisms, and then return aboard Shenzhou 23. Tang, who has flown twice before, would become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong station three times. He said working across language, culture and psychology was the hardest part of this mission, noting that Ali began training knowing almost no Chinese, since the labels and instructions on board are in Chinese.
ourworld.bigPicture: Ali said he hopes this flight is a first step and that cooperation could grow from one astronaut on one flight to several joint flights, and perhaps to the moon and Mars. Whether that happens is not yet known. The mission also comes as China prepares for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030, while NASA aims to land astronauts on the moon in 2028. Flights like this one could show how space programs might work with partner countries, though what comes next has not been announced.
ourworld.originalTitle: China unveils new space mission crew, with a Pakistani astronaut set to board its space station

ourworld.headline: Ice Cap Clues Suggest Warming Halted an Early Start to the Next Ice Age
summary: Researchers studying the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island in Arctic Canada say a new glacial period may have started about 2,000 years ago. The ice cap is a surviving piece of the huge Laurentide Ice Sheet, which once covered much of Canada and the northern United States. Their findings, published in the journal Science, suggest the ice sheet was at its smallest around 3,000 years ago and then began to grow again as temperatures cooled.

To trace this, the team collected ancient plant remains that have emerged from under the ice since it started shrinking in 1960. Because this ice cap is frozen to the bedrock and does not slide, plants buried beneath it stayed in place. Radiocarbon dating showed when the plants were covered, which let the scientists follow how the ice edge advanced. By the 1960s, though, rising summer temperatures meant the ice cap was losing more ice than winter snow could replace, and it began to shrink.
ourworld.bigPicture: The study suggests that human-driven warming may have interrupted a natural climate cycle that was just getting started. The researchers say the early growth would have taken about 30,000 years to rebuild the ice sheet to its former size, so it would not have changed the world quickly. Models suggest the Barnes Ice Cap could vanish within a few centuries, and because past ice sheets helped kick off new glaciation, its loss might affect how future glacial periods develop. The team's view also differs from climate-model studies that placed the next glaciation thousands of years away, partly because scientists define the start of a glacial period differently.
ourworld.originalTitle: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

ourworld.headline: Webb's dust map of Cassiopeia A hints at a star's layers mixing before it exploded
summary: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has produced a detailed mid-infrared view of Cassiopeia A, a well-known supernova remnant. A remnant is the cloud of gas and dust left behind when a massive star explodes. The new data suggests that the inside of the star changed dramatically, possibly only hours before it died. The findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Stars build up layers of different elements as they age, with heavier elements fusing deeper inside. When a star explodes, those elements are scattered and some turn into dust grains. By mapping the makeup of solar-system-sized dust clumps, researchers found signs of a "shell merger," in which layers inside the star mix before the explosion. The team used earlier data from the Spitzer Space Telescope to choose three regions to study. Two lay in a region where an inward-moving shock wave meets debris thrown outward by the blast. One was mostly silica dust and the other mostly carbon dust. The third, called the Green Monster, is rich in magnesium silicates and came from material the star shed before exploding.
ourworld.bigPicture: Reading a star's final hours from dust that has been drifting for hundreds of years gives astronomers a new way to study how massive stars are built. One of the researchers said this understanding is essential for explaining which elements a supernova releases into the galaxy and how they enrich future stars and planets. The study also offers a method that other astronomers could use on different supernova remnants. If it works elsewhere, it might help show how common these late-stage mixing events are, though that remains to be seen.
ourworld.originalTitle: Webb finds evidence star's layers may have merged just hours before Cas A supernova

ourworld.headline: Strong El Niño expected to worsen heat and drought in parts of Africa
summary: A strong El Niño is developing in the Pacific. It is expected to grow stronger toward the end of 2026 and last into early 2027. In parts of Africa, it is expected to make dangerous heat worse and bring severe drought. That could mean more heat-related illness and deaths, tighter water supplies, and more disruption to electricity, food and essential services.

The article was written by a researcher who studies heat waves and health. She explains that heat danger depends on more than air temperature. Humidity, sunlight and wind also affect how well the body can cool itself. Older people, infants, pregnant women, people with chronic illnesses and outdoor workers are especially vulnerable. Poorly ventilated homes and limited access to electricity or cooling can keep people dangerously hot, even at night. Where health records are weak, some heat-related deaths may go uncounted.
ourworld.bigPicture: El Niño affects weather around the world, but the risks may be greatest where extreme heat meets limited access to water, electricity and health care. Because El Niño can be tracked months in advance, early warnings could give governments a chance to act sooner. The author says that with the right preparations, many heat-related illnesses and deaths could be prevented. How much harm actually occurs may depend on how quickly warnings are turned into practical steps and funding.
ourworld.originalTitle: Super El Niño will add to Africa's heat crisis—how governments can protect people before it peaks

wellbeing.headline: Disrupted sleep or sleeping 9+ hours after 50 linked to shorter working lives
summary: A large Finnish study found that sleep habits after age 50 may be linked to how long people stay in paid work. Researchers looked at two Finnish studies, one with 70,339 public sector employees and another with 6,071 working-age adults. They estimated working life expectancy between ages 50 and 68, using sleep survey answers and national employment records.

People with moderate sleep problems were expected to work nearly 5 fewer months than those with none, and those with severe problems about 8 fewer months. Sleeping 9 or more hours a night was linked to roughly 9 fewer months of work in one study and just over 30 fewer months in the other, compared with sleeping 7 to 8½ hours. The researchers found no clear difference between short sleepers and mid-range sleepers. Because the work was observational, it cannot show that sleep directly affects how long people work, and it could not account for factors such as physical and mental health, medical conditions, risky health behaviors or shift work.
wellbeing.bigPicture: Many countries have raised retirement ages, so more people are expected to keep working later in life. The findings suggest that supporting sleep health in midlife could be one useful consideration, especially for people with lower socioeconomic status. The researchers mention possibilities such as cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia through occupational health services, or workplace programs that educate people about sleep. More research would be needed to know whether improving sleep actually changes how long people stay employed.
wellbeing.originalTitle: Sleeping 9 hours a night after 50 may be a surprising warning sign

wellbeing.headline: Regular Coffee Drinking Linked to Differences in Gut Bacteria and Digestive Function
summary: Researchers at the University of Copenhagen studied how regular coffee drinking relates to what happens inside the digestive system. Participants swallowed a small electronic capsule that recorded data as it travelled through the gut, including transit speed, temperature, acidity and muscle contractions. People who drank one to five cups a day on more than three of eight recorded days counted as frequent coffee drinkers, and everyone else formed the comparison group.

Frequent coffee drinkers had a greater variety of gut microorganisms, which fits with earlier research. They also had more acidic conditions in the small intestine and more muscular contractions in the colon. Those contractions help move material through the digestive system. The team notes that it is not yet clear whether the higher acidity is good or bad for health.
wellbeing.bigPicture: Many people deal with constipation and irregular bowel movements, so understanding how coffee affects digestion could be useful. The researchers say the next step would be a controlled study in which participants' coffee intake is regulated, comparing periods of high consumption with periods of none. If that work confirms a direct effect, it might point toward natural ways of encouraging gut movement. For now, the findings show an association and do not offer health advice.
wellbeing.originalTitle: Your daily coffee may be changing your gut in surprising ways

wellbeing.headline: Large study finds exercise for fun and physical work may relate differently to dementia risk
summary: Researchers at the University of Southern California looked at 74 earlier studies covering more than 4.2 million people aged 45 to 93 in 30 countries. They followed diagnoses of dementia, Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia over a median of 10 years. The work was published in The Lancet Public Health.

People who did more recreational activity, such as walking, cycling, running, swimming or sports, had a 24% lower risk of dementia than the least active people. By contrast, people with more physically demanding jobs had a 20% higher risk. Household chores seemed to help and active commuting seemed to carry a small added risk, but each of these findings rested on very few studies.
wellbeing.bigPicture: This study is observational, so it cannot show that physical work causes dementia, and the authors say it should not discourage anyone from taking an active job. Most studies relied on people reporting their own activity, and most came from high-income countries. The findings suggest that the setting in which people move may matter as much as how much they move. The authors say that could point public health efforts toward safe parks, walking trails, adequate leisure time and fewer harmful workplace exposures, though more research would be needed to know what works.
wellbeing.originalTitle: One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk

wellbeing.headline: Study links screen time at ages 1 and 6 to weaker learning and memory
summary: A study that followed children from age 1 to 8 suggests that the timing of screen use may matter as well as the amount. Children who spent more time on screens in infancy and around the start of elementary school tended to do worse academically at age 9. They also had weaker working memory at age 10.5. Working memory is the ability to briefly hold and use information, which helps children follow instructions, solve math problems and understand sentences.

Researchers from Inserm and the National University of Singapore looked at 502 children in the GUSTO birth cohort. Parents reported screen habits at six points between infancy and middle childhood. The links were strongest at age 1 and age 6, while ages 2 and 3 showed no significant links. Children with more total screen time over childhood also tended to have lower academic scores. The study shows associations only, so it cannot prove that screens caused these outcomes. One possible explanation is that screen time can displace conversation, imaginative play and hands-on exploration.
wellbeing.bigPicture: The findings suggest that healthy screen habits may deserve attention both in infancy and when children start formal schooling, not only in the toddler years. The researchers note that a small difference for one child may not be noticeable, but similar patterns across a large population could mean more children face academic difficulties. Future studies may examine content quality, device types and whether parents watch along with their children. That work could eventually lead to more targeted advice about when and how children use screens, though this remains a possibility rather than a certainty.
wellbeing.originalTitle: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

wellbeing.headline: Is Loneliness a Medical Problem or a Social One? New Study Weighs In
summary: A University of Michigan study, published in Social Problems, looks at how loneliness came to be seen as a health issue. Researchers had linked chronic loneliness and social isolation to illness, earlier death and higher healthcare costs. One estimate in the study compared a lack of social connection to smoking 15 cigarettes a day, and another tied loneliness, isolation and living alone to about a 30% higher risk of premature death. Separate research put the cost of social isolation to Medicare at $6.7 billion a year for older adults' care.

Doctoral student Sofia Hiltner interviewed experts and reviewed more than a decade of media coverage, medical journal articles and academic literature. She found that the health link helped loneliness gain credibility, but it also encouraged the idea that anything affecting health should be handled by the healthcare system. In her view, doctors can screen patients and connect them to services, but they cannot rebuild communities or shorten work hours. She also found that the medical community was at first reluctant to take on loneliness, and that much of the push came from academic researchers, government health officials and insurance companies.
wellbeing.bigPicture: The study suggests that calling loneliness a medical issue can raise awareness and prompt action, but it may also pull attention and resources away from the social conditions that leave people isolated. Hiltner says limited time and money mean one approach could crowd out others, though she also notes that a medical framing may inspire more action than would otherwise happen. She hopes policymakers will look further upstream and consider ways to prevent loneliness before it becomes a health concern. If they do, that could mean giving more thought to community life and the way people live and work, alongside healthcare support.
wellbeing.originalTitle: Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong

wellbeing.headline: Kidney Protein Linked to Phosphate Balance and Blood Vessel Aging in Animal Study
summary: Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine have identified a kidney protein, called TMEM174, that helps control phosphate levels in the blood. In animal models, a shortage of the protein led to faster stiffening of blood vessels and a much shorter lifespan. The effects were strongest when the animals ate a diet high in phosphate, and cutting back on phosphate eased some of the damage. The study was published in October 2026.

Phosphate is a mineral that the body needs, and it is found in meat, fish, grains, nuts, legumes and dairy. It is also added to processed foods and drinks, and the body absorbs these additives more quickly than the phosphates in whole foods. When blood phosphate stays high, cells in blood vessel walls can start depositing bone-like crystals, which hardens the vessels. The researchers think TMEM174 works as a brake on another protein, NPT2A, which pulls phosphate back into the blood after the kidneys filter it.
wellbeing.bigPicture: High blood phosphate is uncommon in the general population but much more common in people with chronic kidney disease, so this finding could matter most for them. The researchers suggest TMEM174 could become a target for future medicines that lower the phosphate the kidneys send back into the blood, though this has not yet been shown in people. Eating fewer processed foods such as fast food, deli meats and sodas may help somewhat, but the senior author notes that diet alone is hard to rely on because phosphate appears in so many foods. Further research is planned to learn more about how these kidney proteins work and why calcium builds up in the blood vessels of people with kidney disease.
wellbeing.originalTitle: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging

wellbeing.headline: Small daily doses of peppermint oil linked to lower blood pressure in small study
summary: Researchers at the University of Lancashire tested whether peppermint oil could help people with mildly raised blood pressure. They recruited 40 adults aged 18 to 65 who had elevated blood pressure or stage 1 hypertension, an early stage of high blood pressure. Participants were randomly placed in one of two groups.

One group took 100 microliters of food-grade peppermint oil a day, about a tenth of a milliliter, split into two doses mixed with water. The other group took a peppermint-flavored placebo without the active compounds. After 20 days, the top number (systolic) in the peppermint group fell from roughly 130 to 122 mmHg, while the placebo group stayed almost the same. After accounting for starting levels, the peppermint group averaged 8.5 mmHg lower. The study appeared in PLOS One.
wellbeing.bigPicture: High blood pressure is a major risk factor for heart disease, and the researchers suggest peppermint oil might one day become a simple, low-cost, well-tolerated option. That remains a possibility, not a conclusion: the study was small and lasted under three weeks. Larger and longer trials are needed to see whether the effect lasts and whether peppermint oil could work alongside existing treatments. The researchers stress that people should not use it to replace prescribed medication, or swallow essential oils not made for oral use.
wellbeing.originalTitle: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days

wellbeing.headline: Brain scans reveal three biological patterns that cut across ADHD and anxiety diagnoses
summary: A study led by Stanford Medicine, published in Nature Mental Health, used brain scans and an AI model to look for biological patterns in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both. The team found three brain types, which they call biotypes. Each one involves disruptions in a different set of brain circuits. The data came from a large U.S. study of children who were 9 or 10 years old when they joined, and the results were checked against scans from another 224 children in a separate project.

The three biotypes are called externalizing-disinhibited, internalizing-distressed and mixed. The first is linked to more impulsivity and rule-breaking and is more often seen with ADHD. The second is tied to guilt, tension, perfectionism and anxiety or depression symptoms, and is more often seen with anxiety. The mixed group had more trouble with attention, irritability and self-injury, and was more likely to have an ADHD diagnosis. Even so, every pairing of biotype and diagnosis turned up among the children studied.
wellbeing.bigPicture: Doctors now diagnose ADHD and anxiety with symptom checklists, even though the two conditions often share symptoms. Adding biological information could someday help clinicians spot these conditions sooner and choose treatments that suit each child, which may reduce the trial and error of trying several medications. The researchers do not expect biotypes to replace symptom-based diagnoses, and they hope future clinical trials will test how different treatments affect each pattern. For now, this is early research, and what it could mean for care is still a possibility rather than a result.
wellbeing.originalTitle: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety

wellbeing.headline: Japanese team tests light-activated egg antibodies to target gum disease bacteria
summary: Researchers at Nagoya University in Japan have developed an experimental gum disease treatment that aims at one harmful bacterium, Porphyromonas gingivalis, and leaves helpful mouth microbes alone. The method pairs antibodies from the egg yolks of hens immunized against the bacterium with a light-sensitive dye. When near-infrared light is shone on the area, the dye activates and damages the bacteria it has attached to. The work was published in the Journal of Translational Medicine.

In lab tests, the treatment attached only to P. gingivalis and did not affect other bacteria or healthy human gum cells. Standard antimicrobial light therapy, by comparison, damaged gum cells and slowed healing. In mice with periodontitis, the new approach significantly reduced loss of the jawbone that supports teeth.
